19214.q: Which particles do acids release when dissolved in water?
19214.e: Acids release hydrogen ions in water. The more of them there are in the solution, the more acidic it is.
19214.m: Acids release hydrogen ions in water.

19215.q: Which rule applies when diluting a concentrated acid?
a: First the water, then the acid
First the acid, then the water
Pour both in quickly at the same time
19215.e: If you pour water into concentrated acid, the strong heat can make it boil suddenly and spray acid. That is why you add the acid slowly to the water.
19215.m: When diluting, always add the acid to the water, never the other way round.

a: A solution of a base in water
19216.e: When a base dissolves in water, it forms an alkali solution. Alkalis are the chemical opposite of acids.
19216.m: An alkali solution is a base dissolved in water.

19217.q: Which household product often contains a strong alkali?
19217.e: Many drain cleaners contain sodium hydroxide. The strong alkali dissolves hair and grease and is corrosive, so you need gloves.
19217.m: Drain cleaners are often strongly corrosive alkalis.

19218.q: What colour does red litmus paper turn in an alkali?
19218.e: Litmus turns blue in basic solutions. This lets you tell alkalis apart from acids.

19219.q: What is the alkali called that forms when sodium hydroxide dissolves in water?
19219.e: Sodium hydroxide in water gives caustic soda solution. It is used, for example, to make soap and pretzels.
19219.m: Sodium hydroxide in water gives caustic soda solution.

19220.q: What is formed when an acid and an alkali come together in the right amounts?
19220.e: This reaction is called neutralisation. The acidic and basic particles cancel each other out.

19221.q: Which particles are typical of alkalis?
19221.e: Alkalis contain many hydroxide ions. They consist of one oxygen atom and one hydrogen atom and are negatively charged.
19221.m: Hydroxide ions make a solution basic.

19223.q: What does a pH value below 7 mean?
19223.e: The lower the pH value, the more acidic a solution is. Values above 7 mean basic.
19223.m: A pH value below 7 means acidic.

19224.q: What range does the usual pH scale cover?
19224.e: The common pH scale goes from 0 to 14. The neutral point is in the middle.
19224.m: The pH scale usually goes from 0 to 14.

19225.q: What colour does universal indicator show in a neutral solution (pH 7)?
19225.e: Universal indicator turns red to orange in acidic solutions and purple in strongly basic ones. At pH 7 it shows a green colour.
19225.m: Universal indicator turns green in neutral solutions.

19227.q: What can you use to find the pH value of a solution easily?
19227.e: Universal indicator is a mixture of dyes that shows a different colour depending on the pH value. You read the value off a colour chart.
19227.m: Universal indicator shows the pH value by its colour.

19228.q: How many times more acidic is a solution with pH 3 than a solution with pH 4?
19228.e: The pH scale is logarithmic. One step lower means ten times more acidic particles, so 10 times more acidic.
19228.m: Each pH step means a difference by a factor of ten.

19229.q: What is the easiest method to separate sand from water?
19229.e: When filtering, the sand stays in the filter paper. The water flows through as the filtrate.
19229.m: Solid particles are separated from liquids by filtering.

19230.q: How do the Swiss Saltworks get salt from brine?
19230.e: Brine is salty water from underground. When it is evaporated, the water turns to vapour and the salt is left behind.

19231.q: What is the easiest way to separate iron filings from sand?
19231.e: Iron is attracted by a magnet, sand is not. This makes it easy to separate the two.
19231.m: Magnetic substances are separated with a magnet.

19232.q: Which property of substances is used in distilling?
19232.e: When distilling, the substance with the lower boiling point evaporates first. The vapour is cooled and collected as a liquid again.
19232.m: Distilling separates liquids by their boiling points.

19233.q: Which method can separate the dyes in a felt-tip pen?
19233.e: In paper chromatography, the dyes travel through the paper with the solvent at different speeds. This separates them visibly.

19234.q: What do you call solid particles settling at the bottom of a liquid?
19234.e: Heavy particles sink because of gravity and settle. Afterwards you can carefully pour off the liquid.
19234.m: In sedimentation, solid particles settle at the bottom.

19235.q: Which separation method takes place when you brew tea?
19235.e: Hot water draws flavours and colours out of the tea leaves. Drawing substances out with a solvent is called extraction.
19235.m: When making tea, substances are extracted.

19336.e: 91 has 9 tens, which is more than all the other numbers.
19336.m: With two-digit numbers, compare the tens first.

19337.m: The next number is always one bigger.

19338.m: The number before is always one smaller.

19339.q: How many tens does the number 47 have?
19339.e: 47 is made up of 4 tens and 7 ones.
19339.m: In a two-digit number, the tens digit comes first.

19340.q: How do you write “fifty-eight” as a number?
19340.e: Fifty is 5 tens and eight is 8 ones, which makes 58.
19340.m: You write the tens first and then the ones.

19341.q: Which number is exactly halfway between 10 and 20?
19341.e: From 10 to 15 is 5 steps, and from 15 to 20 is also 5 steps.
19341.m: The middle is the same distance from both sides.

19342.e: 19 has only 1 ten, 25 has 2 tens, so 19 is smaller.
19342.m: Fewer tens means a smaller number.

19343.q: How many fingers do you have on both hands together?
19343.e: Each hand has 5 fingers, and 5 + 5 makes 10.
19343.m: Our ten fingers help us count.

19344.q: How many days are there in a week?
19344.e: The week has the days Monday to Sunday, which is 7 days.

19345.q: How many months are there in a year?
19345.e: From January to December you count 12 months.

19346.q: How many legs do 3 hens have altogether?
19346.e: Each hen has 2 legs, so 2 + 2 + 2 makes 6.

19347.q: Lena is counting backwards: 10, 9, 8, 7. Which number does she say next?
19347.e: When counting backwards, each number is 1 smaller, so after 7 comes 6.
19347.m: Counting backwards means always saying one less.

19348.q: How many wheels do 2 bikes have altogether?
19348.e: A bike has 2 wheels, and 2 + 2 makes 4.

19349.q: How many letters are there in the word “school”?
19349.e: You count s, c, h, o, o, l, which is 6 letters.
19349.m: When counting letters, point to each one separately.

19350.m: When adding past ten, first make up to ten.

19351.m: First up to ten, then add the rest.

19352.e: 2 tens and 3 tens are 5 tens, which is 50.
19352.m: Add tens like small numbers with a zero on the end.

19353.e: You only add the ones together, 4 + 5 makes 9, so 39.
19353.m: Ones are added to the ones.

19354.e: You add the tens together, 40 + 20 makes 60, then add the 5 ones, so 65.
19354.m: Tens are added to the tens.

19355.m: A number plus itself makes double.

19356.q: Tim has 12 marbles and gets 7 more. How many marbles does he have now?
19356.m: When something is added, you do a plus sum.

19357.m: You can add the tens first and then the ones.

19358.m: When taking away, first go back to ten.

19359.m: You can split the number you take away into two parts.

19360.e: 6 tens minus 2 tens are 4 tens, which is 40.
19360.m: Take away tens like small numbers.

19361.e: For the ones you work out 6 − 4, which makes 2, so 32.
19361.m: Ones are taken away from the ones.

19362.m: Take away the tens first and then the ones.

19363.q: A bus has 20 passengers. At the bus stop, 6 get off. How many passengers are left on the bus?
19363.m: When something goes away, you do a minus sum.

19364.m: Minus one always gives the number before.

19365.m: Take away bigger numbers in steps.

19366.m: Multiplying is adding the same number several times.

19367.m: Five times five is part of the times tables.

19369.e: 10 times 7 makes 70; you add a zero to the 7.
19369.m: When you multiply by ten, you add a zero.

19370.q: A box holds 6 eggs. How many eggs are in 3 boxes?
19370.e: 3 boxes with 6 eggs each is 3 times 6, which is 18.
19370.m: You count equal groups together by multiplying.

19371.e: 4 times 9 makes 36, because 2 times 9 is 18 and double that is 36.
19371.m: Times four is double the double.

19372.e: If you take something 0 times, you have nothing, so 0.
19372.m: Any number times zero makes zero.

19373.e: 10 divided into 2 equal parts makes 5, because 2 times 5 makes 10.

19374.e: 3 times 7 makes 21, so 21 divided by 3 is 7.
19374.m: The times tables help with dividing.

19375.e: 4 times 5 makes 20, so 20 divided by 4 makes exactly 5.
19375.m: Dividing is the opposite of multiplying.

19376.q: 24 apples are shared fairly between 6 children. How many apples does each child get?
19376.e: 24 divided by 6 makes 4, because 6 times 4 makes 24.

19377.e: 10 times 3 makes 30, so 30 divided by 10 makes exactly 3.
19377.m: When dividing by ten, the zero at the end disappears.

19378.m: You find half of a number by dividing by two.

19379.q: 16 children make groups of four. How many groups are there?
19379.e: 16 divided by 4 makes 4, because 4 times 4 makes 16.
19379.m: When splitting into groups, you divide.

19380.q: What comes next in the sequence: 5, 10, 15, 20, ...?
19380.e: Each number is 5 bigger than the one before, 20 + 5 makes 25.
19380.m: In a number sequence, first look for the rule.

19381.q: What comes next in the sequence: 3, 6, 9, 12, ...?
19381.e: The numbers always get 3 bigger, 12 + 3 makes 15.
19381.m: The three times table always jumps on by three.

19382.q: What comes next in the sequence: 20, 18, 16, 14, ...?
19382.e: The numbers always get 2 smaller, 14 − 2 makes 12.
19382.m: A sequence can also get smaller.

19383.q: What comes next in the sequence: 1, 3, 5, 7, ...?
19383.e: The numbers always jump on by 2, 7 + 2 makes 9.
19383.m: Equal jumps make a sequence regular.

19384.q: What comes next in the sequence: 10, 20, 30, 40, ...?
19384.m: In steps of ten, only the tens digit changes.

19385.q: What comes next in the sequence: 1, 2, 4, 8, ...?
19385.e: Each number is doubled, and double 8 is 16.

19386.q: What comes next in the sequence: 100, 90, 80, 70, ...?
19386.e: The numbers always get 10 smaller, 70 − 10 makes 60.
19386.m: Counting back in tens makes the tens digit smaller.

19387.q: Which of these numbers is even?
19387.e: 14 can be divided by 2 with no remainder, because 7 + 7 makes 14.

19388.q: Which of these numbers is odd?
19388.e: 21 ends in 1 and leaves a remainder when divided by 2.

19389.q: How can you recognise an even number?
a: It divides by 2 with no remainder
19389.e: An even number can be split into two equal parts with nothing left over.
19389.m: Even numbers can be halved with no remainder.

19390.q: What is the smallest even number that is bigger than 10?
19390.e: 11 is odd, the next even number after 10 is 12.
19390.m: Even numbers follow each other in steps of two.

19391.q: How many even numbers are there from 1 to 10?
19391.e: The even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, which is 5 numbers.
19391.m: Even and odd numbers always take turns.

19392.q: Which odd number comes straight after 15?
19392.e: 16 is even, then comes the odd number 17.
19392.m: Between two odd numbers there is always an even number.

19393.e: 33 ends in 3, and 3 is an odd digit.
19393.m: The last digit tells you whether a number is even.

19394.q: How many corners does a triangle have?
19394.e: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners; that is where its name comes from.
19394.m: The name triangle tells you the number of corners.

19395.q: How many sides does a rectangle have?
19395.e: A rectangle has one side each at the top and bottom and one side each on the left and right, which is 4 sides.
19395.m: In a rectangle, opposite sides are the same length.

19396.e: A circle is completely round and so has not a single corner.
19396.m: A circle is round and has no corners.

19397.q: Which shape has 4 sides of equal length and 4 right angles?
19397.e: In a square, all 4 sides are the same length and all corners are right angles.
19397.m: A square is a rectangle with sides of equal length.

19398.q: How many sides does a hexagon have?
19398.e: A hexagon has 6 corners and so also 6 sides.
19398.m: Polygons have as many sides as corners.

19399.q: What shape are the faces of a cube?
19399.e: A cube has 6 faces, and each of them is a square.
19399.m: A cube is made of six squares.

19400.q: What shape is the stop sign on the road?
19400.e: The red stop sign has 8 corners and is an octagon.
19400.m: You can recognise the stop sign by its eight corners.

19401.q: How many seconds are there in a minute?
19401.e: A minute lasts 60 seconds; that is how long the second hand takes to go round once.

19402.q: How many hours are there in a day?
19402.e: A whole day including the night lasts 24 hours.

19403.q: The big hand is on the 12 and the little hand is on the 3. What time is it?
19403.e: The little hand shows the hour, and the big hand on the 12 means it is exactly on the hour.
19403.m: The little hand shows the hours, the big hand the minutes.

19404.q: How many minutes are there in half an hour?
19404.m: Half an hour lasts thirty minutes.

19405.q: It is 8 o'clock. What time is it 2 hours later?
19405.e: You count on 2 hours, 8 + 2 makes 10, so 10 o'clock.
19405.m: For a later time, you add the hours.

19406.q: How many minutes are there in a quarter of an hour?
19406.e: A quarter of 60 minutes is 15 minutes, because 4 times 15 makes 60.
19406.m: A quarter of an hour lasts fifteen minutes.

19407.q: School starts at 8 o'clock. Lina gets there 20 minutes early. What time does she arrive?
19407.e: 20 minutes before 8 o'clock is 7 o'clock and 40 minutes, because 60 − 20 makes 40.
19407.m: Earlier means taking time away from the clock time.

19408.q: You have a 2-franc coin and a 1-franc coin. How much money do you have?
19408.e: 2 francs and 1 franc make 3 francs altogether.
19408.m: You count money by adding up the values.

19409.q: A croissant costs 2 francs. How much do 3 croissants cost?
19409.m: For several of the same thing, you multiply the price by the number.

19410.q: You pay for an exercise book that costs 3 francs with 5 francs. How much change do you get?
19410.m: The change is the money you paid minus the price.

19411.q: How much are 50 centimes and 50 centimes together?
19411.e: 50 + 50 makes 100 centimes, and 100 centimes are 1 franc.
19411.m: Two 50-centime coins together are worth one franc.

19412.q: Which Swiss coin is worth the most?
19412.e: The 5-franc coin is the Swiss coin with the highest value.
19412.m: The biggest Swiss coin is the 5-franc coin.

19413.q: An apple costs 80 centimes and a banana 70 centimes. How much do both cost together?
19413.e: 80 + 70 makes 150 centimes, which is 1 franc and 50 centimes.
19413.m: You swap a hundred centimes for one franc.

19414.e: 5 times 20 centimes makes 100 centimes, which is 1 franc.
19414.m: Five 20-centime coins together are worth one franc.

19415.q: How many centimetres are there in a metre?
19415.m: A metre has a hundred centimetres.

19416.q: What is the best way to measure how long an exercise book is?
19416.e: A ruler has a scale in centimetres, and you use it to measure lengths.
19416.m: You measure lengths with a ruler or a folding rule.

19417.q: How many metres are there in a kilometre?
19417.e: 1 kilometre is a long distance of 1000 metres, about 10 football pitches end to end.
19417.m: A kilometre is a thousand metres long.

19418.e: 99, 90 and 50 centimetres are all shorter than a whole metre, so 1 metre is the longest.
19418.m: To compare, convert all lengths into the same unit.

19419.q: Two ribbons are 40 centimetres and 25 centimetres long. How long are they together?
19419.e: 40 + 25 makes 65, so both ribbons together are 65 centimetres long.
19419.m: You can simply add the same units together.

19420.q: Which unit fits the length of a pencil?
19420.e: A pencil is about 15 to 20 centimetres long, so centimetres fit.
19420.m: Short things are measured in centimetres.

19421.q: How many millimetres are there in a centimetre?
19421.e: 1 centimetre is divided into 10 small millimetres.

19422.q: How many grams are there in a kilogram?
19422.e: A kilogram weighs exactly the same as 1000 grams together.
19422.m: A kilogram has a thousand grams.

19423.q: What do you use to measure how heavy something is?
19423.e: Scales show how heavy an object is.

19424.q: Which is heavier, 1 kilogram of feathers or 1 kilogram of stones?
19424.e: Both weigh exactly 1 kilogram; the feathers just take up much more space.
19424.m: The same number of kilograms always weighs the same.

19425.q: Which unit fits the weight of an apple?
19425.e: An apple weighs about 150 to 200 grams, so grams fit.
19425.m: Light things are weighed in grams.

19426.q: How much do 3 bags of flour weigh if each weighs 2 kilograms?
19426.m: Things of the same weight can be added up by multiplying.

19427.e: 950, 800 and 500 grams are all less than a whole kilogram, so 1 kilogram is the greatest.
19427.m: To compare, convert kilograms into grams.

19428.q: A dog weighs 8 kilograms and a cat 4 kilograms. How much heavier is the dog?
19428.e: 8 − 4 makes 4, so the dog is 4 kilograms heavier.
19428.m: You find the difference by taking away.

19429.q: Anna is taller than Ben. Ben is taller than Carla. Who is the shortest?
19429.e: Anna is taller than Ben and Ben is taller than Carla, so Carla is the shortest.
19429.m: In comparison puzzles, put everyone in order.

19430.q: Today is Monday. Which day is the day after tomorrow?
19430.e: Tomorrow is Tuesday, and the day after tomorrow is the day after that, so Wednesday.
19430.m: The day after tomorrow comes one day after tomorrow.

19431.q: 5 children are standing in a line. Mia is standing exactly in the middle. How many children are in front of her?
19431.e: With 5 children, Mia is in 3rd place, so there are 2 children in front of her.
19431.m: In the middle, there are the same number on both sides.

19432.q: I am a number. If you add 3, you get 10. Which number am I?
19432.e: You work backwards, 10 − 3 makes 7, and 7 + 3 really does make 10.
19432.m: You often solve a number puzzle by working backwards.

19433.q: A farmer has 3 cows and 2 hens. How many legs do the animals have altogether?
19433.e: 3 cows have 3 times 4, so 12 legs; 2 hens have 4 legs; together that is 16.
19433.m: With mixed animals, count each kind separately.

19434.q: Tom is 6 years old. His sister is 3 years older. How old is she?
19434.m: Whoever is older has more years.

19435.q: A box contains only red and blue balls. There are 9 balls, 4 of them red. How many blue balls are there?
19435.e: All the balls that are not red are blue, so you work out 9 − 4 and get 5.
19435.m: You find the missing part by taking the known part away from the whole.

19436.e: You give both fractions the denominator 6: 3/6 + 2/6 makes 5/6.
19436.m: You only add fractions once they have the same denominator.

19437.e: Numerator times numerator and denominator times denominator: 6/20, simplified 3/10.
19437.m: When multiplying, you multiply numerator by numerator and denominator by denominator.

19438.e: You multiply by the reciprocal: 2/3 · 9/4 makes 18/12, simplified 3/2.
19438.m: To divide by a fraction, you multiply by its reciprocal.

19439.q: What is the fraction 18/24 in its simplest form?
19439.e: The highest common factor of 18 and 24 is 6. 18 ÷ 6 makes 3 and 24 ÷ 6 makes 4.
19439.m: You simplify fully using the highest common factor.

19440.q: Which of these fractions is the biggest?
19440.e: As decimals: 5/6 is about 0.833, 4/5 is 0.8, 7/9 is about 0.778 and 3/4 is 0.75.
19440.m: Fractions are easiest to compare with the same denominator or as decimals.

19441.q: There are 35 children in a class, and 2/5 of them cycle to school. How many is that?
19441.e: One fifth of 35 is 7, two fifths are 2 · 7, which makes 14.
19441.m: To work out a fraction of an amount, divide by the denominator and multiply by the numerator.

19442.q: How do you write the improper fraction 17/5 as a mixed number?
19442.e: 17 ÷ 5 makes 3 remainder 2. So it is 3 wholes and 2/5.
19442.m: An improper fraction has a numerator bigger than its denominator.

19443.q: Which decimal is equal to the fraction 3/8?
19443.m: You turn a fraction into a decimal by dividing the numerator by the denominator.

19444.e: 25 · 4 makes 100. Together the factors have two decimal places, so 1.00.
19444.m: The result has as many decimal places as both factors together.

19445.e: You move the decimal point one place in both numbers: 72 ÷ 3 makes 24.
19445.m: When dividing, move the decimal point the same number of places in both numbers.

19446.q: Which of these numbers is the smallest?
19446.e: Comparing place by place, 0.09 has a 0 in the tenths place and a 9 in the hundredths place; 0.099 is 9 thousandths bigger.
19446.m: Compare decimals place by place from left to right.

19447.q: What is 3.14159 rounded to two decimal places?
19447.e: The third decimal place is a 1, so you round down.
19447.m: From the digit 5 upwards you round up; below it you round down.

19448.q: Which fraction gives a recurring decimal?
19448.e: 1 ÷ 3 makes 0.333..., the 3 repeats forever. The others make 0.25, 0.2 and 0.125.
19448.m: A recurring decimal has digits that repeat forever.

19449.q: Lea buys a book for CHF 12.50, an exercise book for CHF 7.80 and pens for CHF 3.95. How much does she pay?
19449.m: In written addition, the decimal points go exactly underneath each other.

19450.m: You work out a percentage as the whole amount times the percentage divided by 100.

19451.q: A jumper costs CHF 120 and is reduced by 20 %. How much does it cost now?
19451.m: After a 20 % reduction, you still pay 80 % of the price.

19452.q: In a test, Nino scores 18 out of 24 points. What percentage is that?
19452.m: You work out a percentage as the part divided by the whole times 100.

19453.q: 30 % of a number is 45. What is the number?
19453.e: If 30 % is 45, then 10 % is 15. So 100 % is 150.
19453.m: You find the whole amount via the value of 1 % or 10 %.

19454.q: A price of CHF 200 rises by 10 % and then falls by 10 %. What is it at the end?
19454.m: An increase and an equal percentage decrease do not cancel each other out.

19456.q: There is CHF 5,000 in a savings account at 2 % interest per year. How much interest is paid after one year?
19456.m: The yearly interest is a percentage of the capital.

19457.e: From -7 you go 12 steps to the right on the number line and land on 5.
19457.m: Adding a positive number means going right on the number line.

19458.e: Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its absolute value: 3 + 8 makes 11.
19458.m: Subtracting a negative number means adding its absolute value.

19459.e: The product of two negative numbers is positive: 6 · 4 makes 24.
19459.m: If two factors have the same sign, the product is positive.

19460.e: 36 ÷ 9 makes 4. The signs are different, so the result is negative.
19460.m: If two numbers have different signs, their quotient is negative.

19461.q: In the morning the thermometer in Samedan shows -9 °C, at midday 4 °C. By how many degrees has it got warmer?
19461.e: The difference is 4 − (-9), which makes 13 degrees.
19461.m: You work out a temperature difference as the later value minus the earlier value.

19462.q: Which of these negative numbers is the smallest?
19462.e: On the number line, -8 is furthest to the left. The bigger the absolute value of a negative number, the smaller it is.
19462.m: Negative numbers are smaller the further left they are on the number line.

19463.q: What is (-2) to the power of 3?
19463.e: (-2) · (-2) · (-2): the first two make 4, times -2 makes -8.
19463.m: A negative number with an odd exponent stays negative.

19464.q: Which of these numbers is a prime number?
19464.e: 29 can only be divided by 1 and itself. 27 can be divided by 3, 33 by 3 and 11, and 39 by 3 and 13.
19464.m: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.

19465.q: What is the only even prime number?
19465.e: Every other even number can be divided by 2 and so has more than two factors.
19465.m: All prime numbers except 2 are odd.

19466.q: Why is the number 1 not a prime number?
a: Because it has only one factor
Because it is a square number
19466.e: A prime number needs exactly two different factors. The number 1 has only the factor 1.
19466.m: The number 1 is neither a prime number nor a composite number.

19467.q: How many prime numbers are there between 1 and 20?
19467.e: They are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19, so 8 prime numbers.
19467.m: The smallest prime numbers are 2, 3, 5 and 7.

19468.q: What is the prime factorisation of 180?
19468.e: 180 makes 2 · 90, 90 makes 2 · 45, 45 makes 3 · 15 and 15 makes 3 · 5. So 2 · 2 · 3 · 3 · 5.
19468.m: Every natural number greater than 1 can be broken down into prime factors in exactly one way.

19469.q: Which method finds all prime numbers up to a certain limit by crossing out multiples?
19469.e: With the sieve of Eratosthenes, you cross out all multiples of 2, 3, 5 and so on in turn. The prime numbers are what is left.
19469.m: The sieve of Eratosthenes goes back to an ancient Greek scholar.

19470.q: Which pair of numbers are twin primes?
19470.e: Twin primes are two prime numbers that are 2 apart. 15, 9 and 21 are not prime numbers.
19470.m: Twin primes are prime numbers that differ by exactly 2.

19471.q: Which of these numbers is divisible by 9?
19471.e: The digit sum of 7254 is 7 + 2 + 5 + 4, which is 18, and 18 is divisible by 9.
19471.m: A number is divisible by 9 if its digit sum is divisible by 9.

19472.q: Which of these numbers is divisible by 4?
19472.e: The last two digits, 16, form a number that is divisible by 4.
19472.m: A number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits form a number divisible by 4.

19473.q: What is the highest common factor (HCF) of 48 and 36?
19473.e: The factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Of these, 12 is the biggest that also divides 48.
19473.m: The HCF is the biggest number that divides both numbers with no remainder.

19474.q: What is the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 6 and 8?
19474.e: Multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24. 24 is the first one that is also divisible by 6.
19474.m: The LCM is the smallest number that is a multiple of both numbers.

19475.q: How many factors does the number 36 have?
19475.e: The factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 36, so 9 factors.
19475.m: Square numbers always have an odd number of factors.

19476.q: How can you tell that a number is divisible by 5?
19476.e: Every multiple of 5 ends in 0 or 5, for example 35, 70 or 125.
19476.m: A number is divisible by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5.

19477.q: A bus leaves every 12 minutes, a tram every 18 minutes. At 8:00 both leave at the same time. When do they next leave at the same time?
19477.e: You need the LCM of 12 and 18, which is 36. So after 36 minutes, at 8:36.
19477.m: The lowest common multiple helps you find the next shared event.

19478.q: In a triangle, two angles measure 65° and 48°. How big is the third angle?
19478.e: The angles in a triangle add up to 180°. 180° − 65° − 48° makes 67°.
19478.m: The angles in a triangle always add up to 180 degrees.

19479.q: What do the angles in a quadrilateral add up to?
19479.e: A quadrilateral can be split into two triangles by a diagonal: 2 · 180° makes 360°.
19479.m: In every quadrilateral, the interior angles add up to 360 degrees.

19480.q: What do you call an angle that is bigger than 90° and smaller than 180°?
19480.e: Acute angles are smaller than 90°, and a straight angle measures exactly 180°. Obtuse angles lie in between.
19480.m: An obtuse angle lies between a right angle and a straight angle.

19481.q: A right-angled triangle has two shorter sides of 3 cm and 4 cm. How long is the hypotenuse?
19481.e: According to Pythagoras' theorem, 3² + 4² makes 9 + 16, which is 25. The square root of 25 is 5.
19481.m: In a right-angled triangle, the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the hypotenuse.

19482.q: What is a quadrilateral with four sides of equal length whose angles are not right angles called?
19482.e: A rhombus (also called a diamond) has four sides of equal length. If all its angles are also right angles, it is a square.
19482.m: Every square is a special rhombus.

19483.q: What do the angles in a hexagon add up to?
19483.e: The angles in a polygon with n corners add up to (n − 2) · 180°. For n equal to 6: 4 · 180° makes 720°.
19483.m: With each extra corner, the angle sum grows by 180 degrees.

19484.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
19484.e: A square has two lines of symmetry through the midpoints of its sides and two along its diagonals.
19484.m: A rectangle that is not a square has only two lines of symmetry.

19485.q: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 7 m wide. What is its area?
19485.e: The area of a rectangle is length times width: 12 m · 7 m makes 84 m².
19485.m: You work out the area of a rectangle as length times width.

19486.q: A triangle has a base of 10 cm and a height of 6 cm. What is its area?
19486.e: The area of a triangle is base times height divided by 2: 10 · 6 ÷ 2 makes 30 cm².
19486.m: A triangle is half the size of a rectangle with the same base and height.

19487.q: A trapezium has parallel sides of 8 cm and 4 cm and a height of 5 cm. What is its area?
19487.e: The area of a trapezium is (a + c) ÷ 2 · h, so (8 + 4) ÷ 2 · 5, which makes 6 · 5 and so 30 cm².
19487.m: For a trapezium, multiply the average of the parallel sides by the height.

19488.q: How many square centimetres are there in a square metre?
19488.e: A metre has 100 cm, so a square metre has 100 · 100, which makes 10,000 cm².
19488.m: For area units, the conversion factor between m² and dm² is 100.

19489.q: What is the area of a circle with a radius of 5 cm (rounded)?
19489.e: The area of a circle is π · r². 3.14159 · 25 makes about 78.5 cm².
19489.m: You work out the area of a circle as pi times the radius squared.

19490.q: How many square metres are there in a hectare?
19490.e: A hectare is a square of 100 m by 100 m, so 10,000 m².
19490.m: A hectare is a bit bigger than a football pitch.

19491.q: A square has an area of 64 cm². What is its perimeter?
19491.e: The side length is the square root of 64, so 8 cm. The perimeter is 4 · 8 cm, which makes 32 cm.
19491.m: You get the side length of a square from its area with the square root.

19492.q: A cuboid is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. What is its volume?
19492.e: The volume of a cuboid is length times width times height: 5 · 4 · 3 makes 60 cm³.
19492.m: You work out the volume of a cuboid as length times width times height.

19493.q: What is the volume of a cube with edges 3 cm long?
19493.e: For a cube, you work out the edge to the power of 3: 3 · 3 · 3 makes 27 cm³.
19493.m: The volume of a cube is the edge length to the power of three.

19494.q: How many litres fit into a cubic metre?
19494.e: A litre is the same as a cubic decimetre, and a cubic metre has 10 · 10 · 10, which makes 1,000 dm³.
19494.m: A litre is the same as a cubic decimetre.

19495.q: How many millilitres are equal to one cubic centimetre?
19495.e: A litre has 1,000 ml and 1,000 cm³. That is why 1 cm³ is exactly 1 ml.
19495.m: A cubic centimetre holds exactly one millilitre.

19496.q: An aquarium is 50 cm long, 30 cm wide and 40 cm high. How many litres of water fit into it?
19496.e: 50 · 30 · 40 makes 60,000 cm³. That is 60,000 ml or 60 litres.
19496.m: To get litres, divide cubic centimetres by 1,000.

19497.q: What is the volume of a cylinder with a radius of 2 cm and a height of 10 cm (rounded)?
19497.e: The volume is the base area times the height: π · 2² · 10 makes 40π, about 125.7 cm³.
19497.m: The volume of a cylinder is the area of the circle times the height.

19498.q: All the edges of a cube are doubled. How does its volume change?
19498.e: The volume depends on three edges: 2 · 2 · 2 gives a factor of 8.
19498.m: If you double all the lengths of a solid, its volume becomes eight times as big.

19499.q: In which quadrant is the point (-3, 5)?
19499.e: The x value is negative and the y value is positive. That is top left, so the 2nd quadrant.
19499.m: The quadrants are numbered anticlockwise starting at the top right.

19500.q: What is the horizontal axis in a coordinate system called?
19500.e: The horizontal axis is the x-axis (abscissa), the vertical one is the y-axis (ordinate).
19500.m: For a point, you always give the x value first and then the y value.

19501.q: What are the coordinates of the origin of a coordinate system?
19501.e: The origin is where the two axes cross. There, x and y are both 0.
19501.m: The x-axis and the y-axis cross at the origin.

19502.q: Which point is exactly halfway between A(2, 3) and B(8, 7)?
19502.e: You take the average each time: (2 + 8) ÷ 2 makes 5 and (3 + 7) ÷ 2 makes 5.
19502.m: You find the midpoint of a line segment using the averages of the coordinates.

19503.q: The point P(4, -2) is reflected in the x-axis. Where is the image point?
19503.e: When reflecting in the x-axis, the x value stays the same and the y value changes its sign.
19503.m: When reflecting in the x-axis, only the y value changes its sign.

19504.q: How far apart are the points A(1, 2) and B(7, 10) (in units)?
19504.e: The differences are 6 and 8. With Pythagoras: the square root of 36 + 64, so of 100, makes 10.
19504.m: Distances in a coordinate system are worked out with Pythagoras' theorem.

19505.q: Which point lies on the line y = 2x + 1?
19505.e: If you put in x equal to 3, 2 · 3 + 1 gives the value 7. The other points do not satisfy the equation.
19505.m: A point lies on a line if its coordinates satisfy the equation.

19506.q: Which type of chart is best for showing parts of a whole?
19506.e: In a pie chart, the whole circle stands for 100 %, and the sectors show the parts.
19506.m: A pie chart shows how a whole is divided into parts.

19507.q: Which type of chart best shows how the temperature changes over a day?
19507.e: A line graph joins up measurements over time and makes rises and falls visible.
19507.m: Changes over time are shown well with a line graph.

19508.q: In a pie chart, 25 % stands for the cyclists. How big is the angle of this sector?
19508.e: The whole circle is 360°. 25 % of it is 360° ÷ 4, which makes 90°.
19508.m: In a pie chart, 100 % is exactly 360 degrees.

19509.q: Of 30 children, 12 like pizza best. How big is the pizza sector in a pie chart?
19509.m: You work out the sector angle as the fraction times 360 degrees.

19510.q: A bar chart shows break-time rolls sold from Monday to Friday: 4, 7, 5, 8, 6. What is the average per day?
19510.e: The total is 4 + 7 + 5 + 8 + 6, which is 30. Divided by 5 days, that makes 6.
19510.m: You get the average by adding up all the values and dividing by how many there are.

19511.q: What is the median of the values 3, 9, 4, 7 and 5?
19511.e: In order of size: 3, 4, 5, 7, 9. The middle value is 5.
19511.m: The median is the middle value of a list sorted by size.

19512.q: What is a diagram called that uses circles to show what sets have in common and how they differ?
19512.e: In a Venn diagram, each circle stands for a set. The overlap shows what belongs to both sets.
19512.m: A Venn diagram shows intersections of sets.

19513.q: Solve the equation 3x + 5 = 23. What is x?
19513.e: First subtract 5: 3x makes 18. Then divide by 3: x is 6.
19513.m: An equation stays true if you do the same thing to both sides.

19514.q: Solve the equation 4x − 7 = 3x − 9. What is x?
19514.e: Subtract 3x from both sides: x − 7 makes -9. Then add 7: x is -2.
19514.m: You bring all the x terms to one side and all the numbers to the other.

19515.q: For which value of x is x ÷ 7 = 8?
19515.e: You multiply both sides by 7: x is 8 · 7, which is 56.

19516.q: Solve the equation 2(x + 3) = 16. What is x?
19516.e: Divide both sides by 2: x + 3 makes 8. Then subtract 3: x is 5.
19516.m: With brackets, you divide first or multiply out the bracket.

19517.q: Mia is 4 years older than her brother. Together they are 30 years old. How old is her brother?
19517.e: With x for the brother, x + (x + 4) makes 30, so 2x equals 26 and x equals 13.
19517.m: You solve word problems by calling the unknown x and setting up an equation.

19518.e: You collect like terms: 5x − 3x makes 2x, and then add + 2.
19518.m: You may only collect like terms, such as x and x.

19519.q: What are the solutions of the equation x² = 49?
19519.m: A quadratic equation can have two solutions.

19520.q: On a balance, there are 3 balls of equal weight on the left, and 2 such balls and a 12 kg weight on the right. The balance is level. How heavy is one ball?
19520.e: 3x equals 2x + 12. If you take 2 balls off each side, x equals 12 kg is left.
19520.m: A balance that is level behaves like an equation.

19521.q: I think of a number, multiply it by 3 and add 4. The result is 25. Which number did I think of?
19521.m: You often solve number puzzles by working backwards.

19522.q: What is the next number in the sequence 2, 6, 18, 54, ...?
19522.e: Each number is three times the one before: 54 · 3 makes 162.
19522.m: With number sequences, look for the rule that gets you from one number to the next.

19523.q: What is the next number in the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...?
19523.e: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 8 + 13 makes 21. This is the Fibonacci sequence.
19523.m: In the Fibonacci sequence, each number is the sum of the two before it.

19524.q: What is the next number in the sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...?
19524.e: These are the square numbers 1², 2², 3², 4², 5². Next comes 6², which is 36.
19524.m: Square numbers come from multiplying a number by itself.

19525.q: Two numbers add up to 20, and their difference is 6. What is the bigger number?
19525.e: The bigger number is (20 + 6) ÷ 2, which is 13. The smaller one is 7, and 13 − 7 makes 6.
19525.m: With a sum and a difference, the bigger number is half of the two added together.

19526.q: A two-digit number has a digit sum of 9. The tens digit is twice the ones digit. Which number is it?
19526.e: With ones digit e, 2e + e makes 9, so e equals 3. The tens digit is 6, so the number is 63.
19526.m: In digit puzzles, it helps to look at the tens digit and the ones digit separately.

19527.q: On a farm there are hens and rabbits, with 10 heads and 28 legs altogether. How many rabbits are there?
19527.e: If all 10 animals had 2 legs, there would be 20 legs. The 8 extra legs are shared out 2 each among 4 rabbits.
19527.m: In heads-and-legs puzzles, first work it out as if all the animals were the same.

19528.q: What is the probability of rolling a 6 with a normal dice?
19528.e: A dice has 6 equally likely sides, and only one of them shows the 6.
19528.m: Probability is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the number of possible outcomes.

19529.q: What is the probability of rolling an even number with a dice?
19529.e: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6, so 3 out of 6 possibilities. 3/6 simplifies to 1/2.
19529.m: Count the favourable outcomes carefully before you write the fraction.

19530.q: You roll two dice. What is the probability that the total is 7?
19530.e: Of 36 possible pairs, 6 give a total of 7: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1. 6/36 makes 1/6.
19530.m: With two dice there are 36 equally likely outcomes.

19531.q: You toss a coin three times. What is the probability of getting heads three times?
19531.m: For independent events, you multiply the probabilities.

19532.q: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls. What is the probability of drawing a red ball without looking?
19532.e: There are 10 balls, 5 of them red. 5/10 makes 1/2.
19532.m: The more balls of one colour there are in the bag, the more likely you are to draw that colour.

19533.q: What is the probability of an impossible event?
19533.e: Probabilities lie between 0 and 1. An impossible event has 0, a certain event has 1.
19533.m: A certain event has a probability of 1.

19534.q: What is the probability of NOT rolling a 6 with a dice?
19534.e: The opposite of “a 6” has a probability of 1 − 1/6, which is 5/6.
19534.m: The probability of the opposite event is 1 minus the probability of the event.

19535.q: In how many different ways can 3 children line up in a row?
19535.e: There are 3 possibilities for the first place, 2 for the second and 1 for the last: 3 · 2 · 1 makes 6.
19535.m: The number of orders of n things is n factorial.

19544.q: What is the solution of the equation 3x + 7 = 22?
19544.e: You subtract 7 and get 3x equals 15. Dividing by 3 gives x equals 5.
19544.m: With equations, always do the same step on both sides.

19548.q: What is the solution of the equation 2x/3 − 4 = 6?
19548.e: You add 4 and get 2x/3 equals 10. Multiplying by 3/2 gives x equals 15.
19548.m: You remove a fraction in front of the variable by multiplying by its reciprocal.

19593.q: How many different four-digit PIN codes using the digits 0 to 9 are there?
19593.e: Each of the 4 places can be one of 10 digits, and repeats are allowed. That makes 10⁴, which is 10,000.
19593.m: When choosing with repetition and order, you work out n to the power of k.

19598.q: A restaurant offers 3 starters, 4 main courses and 2 desserts. How many different menus with one course from each group are there?
19598.e: By the product rule, you multiply the possibilities: 3 · 4 · 2 makes 24.
19598.m: Independent choices are multiplied by the product rule.

19636.q: What do you need a wheel for?
19636.e: A wheel turns and rolls along the ground. This makes it much easier to move heavy things.
19636.m: With wheels you can move heavy loads more easily.

19637.e: Only a round wheel can roll smoothly. Corners would bump and stop the wheel.
19637.m: A wheel is round so that it rolls well.

19638.e: The wheel was invented about 5,500 years ago. The oldest surviving wooden wheels are over 5,000 years old.
19638.m: The wheel is a very old invention.

19639.q: Where have very old wooden wheels been found in Switzerland?
19639.e: Long ago, houses stood on stilts on the shores of lakes, for example on Lake Zurich. In the damp ground there, old wooden wheels survived for many thousands of years.
19639.m: Stilt house dwellers lived in houses on stilts by the lake.

19640.q: Around which part in the middle does a wheel turn?
19640.e: The axle is a rod in the middle of the wheel. The wheel turns around it.
19640.m: A wheel turns around its axle.

19641.q: What are the thin rods between the middle and the rim of a bike wheel called?
19641.e: The spokes connect the hub in the middle with the rim on the outside. They make the wheel strong and yet light.
19641.m: Spokes make a bike wheel strong and light.

19642.q: What is the rubber part around the outside of a bike wheel?
19642.e: The rubber tyre is filled with air. It cushions bumps and grips the road well.
19642.m: The rubber tyre cushions bumps and gives the wheel grip.

19643.q: What do people in Switzerland usually call a bicycle?
19643.e: In Switzerland people usually say Velo. The word comes from the French “vélo”.
19643.m: In Switzerland you ride a Velo.

19644.q: Who invented the running machine, the forerunner of the bicycle, in 1817?
19644.e: In 1817 Karl Drais rode his wooden running machine in Mannheim. You pushed yourself along the ground with your feet.
19644.m: The running machine was the beginning of the bicycle.

19645.q: What did the first running machine not have yet?
19645.e: The running machine had no pedals yet. You walked while sitting and pushed yourself along with your feet.
19645.m: The first running machine had no pedals yet.

19646.q: How many wheels does a normal bike have?
19646.e: A normal bike has a front wheel and a back wheel. That makes two wheels altogether.
19646.m: A bike has one wheel at the front and one at the back.

19647.q: What should you wear on your head when cycling?
19647.e: A bike helmet protects your head if you fall. It should fit well and be properly fastened.
19647.m: A bike helmet protects your head.

19648.q: What colour is the light at the back of a bike?
19648.e: A bike has a red light at the back and a white one at the front. That way others can see in the dark which way you are going.
19648.m: The light at the back of a bike is red.

19649.q: Who built the first car with a petrol engine in 1886?
19649.e: Carl Benz applied for a patent for his motor car in 1886. It had three wheels and a petrol engine.
19649.m: Carl Benz is seen as the inventor of the car.

19650.q: Who was the first person to drive a long distance in a car, in 1888?
19650.e: In 1888 Bertha Benz drove with her sons from Mannheim to Pforzheim. That was over 100 kilometres.
19650.m: Bertha Benz bravely showed that the car worked.

19651.q: How many wheels does a normal car have?
19651.e: A normal car has two wheels at the front and two at the back. There is often a spare wheel in the boot too.
19651.m: A car usually runs on four wheels.

19652.q: What does an electric car fill up with instead of petrol?
19652.e: An electric car has a big battery. You charge it with electricity at a charging station.
19652.m: An electric car runs on electricity from its battery.

19653.q: What do you steer a car with?
19653.e: When you turn the steering wheel, the front wheels turn. That is how the car goes round a bend.
19653.m: The steering wheel decides the direction.

19654.q: What must you always fasten in a car?
19654.e: The seat belt holds you in place in an accident. In Switzerland you always have to wear it.
19654.m: In a car you always buckle up.

19655.q: Who had cars built on an assembly line from 1913?
19655.e: Henry Ford had his Model T car built on an assembly line. This made cars quicker to finish and cheaper.
19655.m: Cars are made faster on an assembly line.

19656.q: What does a train run on?
19656.e: A train rolls on two steel rails. The rails guide it safely in the right direction.

19657.q: What did the first locomotives run on?
19657.e: In the first locomotives, coal burned and heated water. The steam drove the wheels.
19657.m: The first locomotives ran on steam.

19658.q: What is the name of the first railway that ran entirely within Switzerland?
19658.e: It ran from 1847 and was named after a delicious pastry from Baden. The people of Zurich had it brought to them fresh by train.
19658.m: The Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn is the oldest railway line within Switzerland.

19659.q: Which railway in Switzerland is the steepest cogwheel railway in the world?
19659.e: The Pilatus Railway has run from Alpnachstad up Mount Pilatus since 1889. At its steepest point it climbs at a gradient of 48 per cent.
19659.m: The Pilatus Railway is the steepest cogwheel railway in the world.

19660.q: Which tunnel in Switzerland is the longest railway tunnel in the world?
19660.e: It was opened in 2016 and is about 57 kilometres long. It runs under the Alps to Ticino.
19660.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.

19661.q: Which railway goes to the highest railway station in Europe?
19661.e: The Jungfrau Railway goes up to the Jungfraujoch at 3,454 metres above sea level. A large part of the line runs through a tunnel in the mountain.
19661.m: The highest railway station in Europe is on the Jungfraujoch.

19662.q: Which brothers were the first to fly a powered aeroplane in 1903?
19662.e: Orville and Wilbur Wright flew in the USA in 1903. The first flight lasted only 12 seconds.
19662.m: The Wright brothers made the first powered flight.

19663.q: Which German flew self-built gliders from 1891?
19663.e: Otto Lilienthal jumped off hills with gliders and flew through the air. He learnt about flying by watching birds.
19663.m: Otto Lilienthal learnt to fly from the birds.

19664.q: Which is the largest airport in Switzerland?
19664.e: Zurich Airport is in Kloten. More planes take off and land there than anywhere else in Switzerland.
19664.m: The largest airport in Switzerland is near Zurich.

19665.q: What does an aeroplane have on the left and right so that it can fly?
19665.e: When the aeroplane moves fast, the wings lift it into the air.
19665.m: The wings carry the aeroplane through the air.

19666.q: What is the person who flies an aeroplane called?
19666.e: The pilot sits at the front in the cockpit. The aeroplane is flown from there.

19667.q: What was the name of the Swiss aeroplane that flew around the world on solar power alone?
19667.e: Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg flew around the Earth in it in 2015 and 2016. It didn't have a drop of fuel on board.
19667.m: Solar Impulse flew around the world on solar power alone.

19668.q: Which flying machine has a large rotor on top instead of fixed wings?
19668.e: On a helicopter, a large rotor turns on top. This lets it take off vertically and hover in the air.
19668.m: A helicopter can hover in the air.

19669.q: What holds a ship in place?
19669.e: The anchor is heavy and hooks into the bottom. That way the ship doesn't drift away.
19669.m: The anchor holds a ship in place.

19670.e: The wind blows into the sails. This pushes the ship across the water.
19670.m: A sailing ship moves with wind power.

19671.q: Why doesn't a big steel ship sink?
a: Its hull pushes aside a lot of water
19671.e: The hull is hollow inside and full of air. It pushes so much water aside that the water carries it.
19671.m: A hollow hull lets even heavy ships float.

19672.q: Which famous ship sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg?
19672.e: The Titanic was thought to be unsinkable. On its first voyage to America it hit an iceberg and sank.
19672.m: Even big ships need to be careful at sea.

19673.q: Which old ships with big paddle wheels still sail on Swiss lakes today?
19673.e: Paddle steamers are powered by steam and turn big paddle wheels. You can see them on Lake Lucerne or Lake Geneva, for example.
19673.m: Old paddle steamers still sail on Swiss lakes.

19674.q: What is the front part of a ship called?
19674.e: The bow is at the front, the stern at the back. The bow is pointed so that it cuts well through the water.
19674.m: The bow is at the front of the ship.

19675.q: Who is in command on a ship?
19675.e: The captain is in charge of the ship. Everyone on board has to listen to them.
19675.m: The captain is in charge of the ship.

19676.q: Who applied for a patent for the telephone in 1876?
19676.e: Alexander Graham Bell got a patent for the telephone in the USA in 1876. Other inventors had also worked on similar devices.
19676.m: Alexander Graham Bell made the telephone famous.

19677.q: Which number do you call in Switzerland to call the police?
19677.e: In Switzerland you can reach the police on 117. The call is free, even from a mobile.
19677.m: In Switzerland the police number is 117.

19678.q: Which number do you call in Switzerland for an ambulance?
19678.e: On 144 you reach the ambulance service. It helps with accidents and when someone is seriously ill.
19678.m: In Switzerland you call an ambulance on 144.

19679.q: What do you call a phone that you can take everywhere with you?
19679.e: A mobile phone doesn't need a cable and has a battery. You can make calls with it almost anywhere.
19679.m: You can take a mobile phone everywhere.

19680.q: What do you usually use to operate a smartphone screen?
19680.e: A smartphone screen senses the touch of your finger. You tap and swipe on it.
19680.m: You use a smartphone with your finger.

19681.q: What did people put into a payphone to make a call in the past?
19681.e: In old phone boxes you had to put in coins. Later there were also phonecards.
19681.m: In the past you paid with coins in a phone box.

19682.q: How does a mobile phone call get to the nearest mast?
19682.e: The mobile sends invisible radio waves through the air. A mast picks them up and passes the call on.
19682.m: A mobile phone sends invisible radio waves.

19683.q: What do you use to change channels comfortably from the sofa?
19683.e: The remote control sends invisible signals to the TV. That way you can change the channel without getting up.
19683.m: You control the TV with the remote control.

19684.q: Who was one of the first to show moving television pictures, in London in 1926?
19684.e: John Logie Baird was an inventor from Scotland. In 1926 he showed scientists a television picture of moving faces.
19684.m: John Logie Baird was a television pioneer.

19685.q: What did the pictures on the first televisions look like?
19685.e: The first televisions only showed black, white and shades of grey. Colour television came much later.
19685.m: The first television pictures were black and white.

19686.q: What is the abbreviation for the radio and television of German-speaking Switzerland?
19686.e: SRF stands for Schweizer Radio und Fernsehen (Swiss Radio and Television). It makes programmes for German-speaking Switzerland.
19686.m: SRF makes radio and TV for German-speaking Switzerland.

19687.q: Which event did millions of people watch live on TV in 1969?
19687.e: In 1969 astronauts landed on the Moon. The pictures were shown live all over the world.
19687.m: The Moon landing was a huge television event.

19688.q: What are the tiny dots that make up the picture on a screen called?
19688.e: A picture on a screen is made up of lots of tiny dots. Each dot can light up in a different colour.
19688.m: A screen picture is made up of lots of pixels.

19689.q: What does the word “television” actually mean?
19689.e: With a television you see pictures from places far away. “Tele” means far, so that is where the name comes from.
19689.m: Television shows pictures from far away.

19691.q: What do you use to move the pointer on a computer screen?
19691.e: When you slide the mouse across the desk, the pointer on the screen moves with it. You select something with a click.
19691.m: You control the pointer with the mouse.

19692.q: Where do you type letters on a computer?
19692.e: The keyboard has a key for every letter. When you press it, the letter appears on the screen.
19692.m: You type letters on the keyboard.

19693.q: How big were the first computers?
a: As small as a mobile phone
19693.e: The first computers had lots of big parts. They often filled a whole room.

19694.q: Where was the World Wide Web invented in 1989?
19694.e: A researcher developed it there so that scientists could share knowledge more easily. Today the whole world uses it.
19694.m: The World Wide Web was invented in Switzerland.

19695.q: What should you never tell anyone so that your computer stays safe?
19695.e: You protect your data with your password. Only you and perhaps your parents should know it.

19696.q: Which two digits does a computer use for calculating inside?
19696.e: Inside a computer there is only power on or power off. This is written as 1 and 0.
19696.m: A computer calculates with zeros and ones.

a: A machine that does tasks by itself
19698.e: A robot is a machine with a program. It can use it to carry out work on its own.
19698.m: A robot does work by itself.

19699.q: Which robot cleans the floor at home?
19699.e: A robot vacuum cleaner moves around the flat by itself. It sucks up dust and crumbs from the floor.
19699.m: A robot vacuum cleaner cleans the floor by itself.

19700.q: What are the robot vehicles that drive around on Mars called?
19700.e: Rovers are driving robots with wheels and cameras. They explore the ground on Mars.

19701.q: What does the Czech word “robota”, which “robot” comes from, mean?
19701.e: The writer Karel Čapek used the word robot in a play in 1920. In Czech, “robota” means hard work or forced labour.
19701.m: The word robot comes from Czech.

19702.q: Where do particularly large numbers of robot arms work?
19702.e: In car factories, robot arms weld and paint the cars. They work quickly and very precisely.
19702.m: Robot arms help to build cars.

19703.q: What can a robot see with?
19703.e: A camera is the robot's eye. A computer analyses the pictures.

19704.q: What tells a robot what to do?
19704.e: A program is a list of exact instructions. The robot carries them out step by step.

19705.q: Who made the light bulb practical for everyone around 1879?
19705.e: Thomas Edison improved the light bulb so that it shone for a long time. Other inventors had worked on it before.
19705.m: Thomas Edison made the light bulb famous.

19706.q: What glows in a light bulb?
19706.e: Inside there is a very thin metal filament. When electricity flows through it, it gets hot and glows.
19706.m: In a light bulb a hot wire glows.

19707.q: What does a light bulb need to shine?
19707.e: Without electricity the light bulb stays dark. Only electricity makes the wire glow.

19708.q: Which lamps use much less electricity than light bulbs?
19708.e: LED lamps hardly get hot and produce almost only light. That is why they save a lot of electricity.

19709.q: What happens to a light bulb when it has been on for a while?
19709.e: A light bulb turns most of the electricity into heat and only a little into light. That is why you mustn't touch it.
19709.m: A light bulb that is on is hot.

19710.q: What did many street lamps burn before there was electric light?
19710.e: In many towns, gas lamps used to burn. A lamplighter lit them in the evening.
19710.m: Street lamps used to burn gas.

19712.q: What do you do with a camera?
19712.e: A camera captures light and records a picture. That is how photos and films are made.
19712.m: You take photos with a camera.

19714.q: What did cameras need in the past to record a picture?
19714.e: In the past you put a film into the camera. Afterwards it had to be developed in a photo lab.
19714.m: In the past, photos were taken on film.

19715.q: Where are the photos stored in a digital camera?
19715.e: A digital camera stores pictures as data. For this there is a small memory card in the camera.
19715.m: Digital photos are stored on a memory card.

19716.e: For a selfie you hold the camera yourself and take a photo of yourself. You usually do it with a mobile phone.
19716.m: A selfie is a photo of yourself.

19717.q: What is the part with the glass lenses at the front of a camera called?
19717.e: The lens contains glass lenses. They collect the light and make the picture sharp.
19717.m: The lens is the camera's eye.

19718.q: What helps when taking photos in the dark?
19718.e: The flash makes bright light for a short moment. That way the photo comes out bright even in the dark.
19718.m: The flash makes dark photos bright.

19719.q: What can you use with a long pole to lift a heavy stone?
19719.e: You lay the pole over a stone as a pivot and push down on the long end. That way you need much less force.
19719.m: A long lever saves a lot of force.

19720.q: What do you use to pull heavy loads up on a rope with little force?
19720.e: A pulley system has several wheels that the rope runs over. You have to pull further, but with less force.
19720.m: A pulley system makes heavy loads lighter.

19721.q: What is a ramp called that makes it easier to push things upwards?
19721.e: On a sloping ramp the way is longer, but you need less force. That is why there are ramps for wheelchairs.
19721.m: A ramp makes pushing things up easier.

19722.q: Which simple machine is the blade of an axe?
19722.e: The blade of an axe is thin at the front and thick at the back. That way it pushes the wood apart.

19723.q: What are wheels with teeth that fit into each other called?
19723.e: When one gear wheel turns, it turns the next one too. Gear wheels are found in Swiss watches, for example.

19724.q: What do you use in the garden to move soil on just one wheel?
19724.e: The wheelbarrow carries the weight on its wheel. You only have to lift it by the handles and push.
19724.m: A wheelbarrow makes heavy loads easier to carry.

19725.q: What do simple machines do for us?
19725.e: Simple machines don't need an engine. They help us move heavy things with less force.

19726.q: Who invented a code made of short and long signals?
19726.e: With Morse code, messages were sent over long wires. Short and long signals stand for letters.
19726.m: You can send messages with Morse code.

19727.q: Which ancient Greek is a screw for lifting water named after?
19727.e: Archimedes lived in Syracuse more than 2,200 years ago. He was a famous mathematician and inventor.
19727.m: Archimedes was a great inventor in ancient Greece.

19728.q: Who invented printing with movable type in Mainz around 1450?
19728.e: Gutenberg cast individual letters from metal. This meant books could be made much faster.
19728.m: Gutenberg made books possible for lots of people.

19729.e: After a walk he saw burrs in his dog's fur. He studied the tiny hooks and copied them.

19730.q: Which kitchen gadget is a Swiss invention from 1947?
19730.e: Alfred Neweczerzal from Davos had his “Rex” peeler protected in 1947. With it you can peel potatoes thinly without cutting much away.
19730.m: The peeler is a Swiss invention.

19731.q: Which artist was already drawing flying machines more than 500 years ago?
19731.e: Leonardo da Vinci was a painter and inventor. He drew many machines that nobody could build at the time.
19731.m: Leonardo da Vinci was both an artist and an inventor.

19732.e: Benjamin Franklin studied lightning around 1750. The lightning conductor carries lightning safely into the ground.
19732.m: A lightning conductor protects houses from lightning strikes.

19733.q: Who decisively improved the steam engine from 1769 with a separate condenser?
19733.e: The Scot James Watt let the steam cool in a separate condenser. That way the cylinder didn't have to be heated up again all the time, and the engine used much less coal.
19733.m: James Watt made the steam engine much more efficient.

19734.q: What were the first steam engines used for in England around 1712?
a: To pump water out of mines
19734.e: In 1712 the Englishman Thomas Newcomen built a steam engine that pumped groundwater out of coal mines. Cars, electric light and aeroplanes didn't exist yet.
19734.m: The first steam engines pumped water out of mines.

19735.q: Which form of energy does a steam engine turn into movement?
19735.e: In the boiler, water is heated by burning coal or wood. The heat produces steam, whose pressure drives a movement.
19735.m: A steam engine turns heat into movement.

19736.q: For which physical quantity is the unit watt, named after James Watt, used?
19736.e: The unit of power is called the “watt” in honour of James Watt. One watt means one joule of energy per second.

19737.q: Which major change in the economy and society was strongly driven by the steam engine?
19737.e: From the 18th century, steam engines powered factories, mines and railways. This change began in England and is called the Industrial Revolution.
19737.m: The steam engine was the engine of the Industrial Revolution.

19738.q: Which means of transport was powered by steam engines from about 1830?
19738.e: Steam locomotives like the “Rocket” by George and Robert Stephenson pulled trains in England from about 1830. Soon railways ran all over Europe.
19738.m: Steam engines powered the first railways.

19739.q: Between which places did the first railway entirely on Swiss soil run from 1847?
19739.e: The Swiss Northern Railway opened the line from Zurich to Baden in 1847. It is also called the “Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn”.
19739.m: The first Swiss railway ran from Zurich to Baden.

19740.q: What moves the piston back and forth in a piston steam engine?
19740.e: Hot steam flows alternately onto the two sides of the piston. The steam pressure pushes the piston back and forth like this.
19740.m: Steam pressure drives the piston of a steam engine.

19741.q: Which fuel is burned in an Otto engine?
19741.e: The Otto engine is the petrol engine. It is named after Nikolaus August Otto, who built the four-stroke engine in 1876.
19741.m: An Otto engine is a petrol engine.

19742.q: In a four-stroke engine, which stroke comes straight after intake?
19742.e: The four strokes are called intake, compression, power and exhaust. After intake, the piston squeezes the mixture together.
19742.m: A four-stroke engine takes in, compresses, works and pushes out.

19743.q: How is the fuel ignited in a diesel engine?
a: By the heat of the highly compressed air
By the spark of a spark plug
19743.e: In a diesel engine, air is squeezed so much that it becomes very hot. The injected diesel ignites in it by itself.
19743.m: A diesel engine ignites through hot, compressed air.

19744.q: Who applied for a patent in 1886 for a “motor car” that is seen as the first modern automobile?
19744.e: Carl Benz received the patent for his three-wheeled motor car with a petrol engine in 1886. This patent is seen as the birth certificate of the automobile.
19744.m: Carl Benz's motor car is seen as the first car.

19745.q: Which woman was the first person to drive a long distance in a car, from Mannheim to Pforzheim in 1888?
19745.e: In 1888 Bertha Benz drove about 100 kilometres with her sons. This proved that the car was fit for everyday use.
19745.m: Bertha Benz made the first long car journey.

19746.q: Which gas is produced when petrol is burned and increases the greenhouse effect?
19746.e: Petrol is made of hydrocarbons. When they burn with oxygen, mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour are produced.
19746.m: Combustion engines give off carbon dioxide.

19747.q: Which component turns the up-and-down movement of the pistons into a turning movement?
19747.e: The pistons are connected to the crankshaft by connecting rods. It turns and passes the power on to the gearbox and wheels.
19747.m: The crankshaft turns back-and-forth into rotation.

19748.q: What is the spark plug for in a petrol engine?
a: It ignites the mixture with a spark
It pumps petrol into the tank
19748.e: The spark plug makes an electric spark at the right moment. It ignites the compressed mixture of petrol and air.
19748.m: The spark plug ignites the petrol and air mixture with a spark.

19749.q: What is the fixed part of an electric motor called?
19749.e: The stator stays still and produces a magnetic field. The moving part of the motor turns inside it.
19749.m: In an electric motor the stator does not move.

19750.q: Which energy conversion takes place in an electric motor?
19750.e: An electric motor uses electricity to create rotation with magnetic fields. In this way it powers trains, bikes or fans, for example.
19750.m: An electric motor turns electricity into movement.

19751.q: What is a machine called that does the opposite and produces electricity from turning?
19751.e: A generator works like an electric motor in reverse. When it is turned, electricity is produced by induction.
19751.m: A generator turns movement into electricity.

19752.q: Which scientist discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831?
19752.e: Michael Faraday showed that a changing magnetic field produces electricity in a coil. Generators and transformers are based on this.

19753.q: What does an electric motor need in order to turn?
a: Magnets and electricity flowing through coils
19753.e: When electricity flows through a coil, it becomes a magnet itself. The attraction and repulsion between coil and magnets makes the motor turn.
19753.m: An electric motor turns because of magnetic forces.

19754.q: What powers almost all SBB trains today?
19754.e: The Swiss rail network is almost completely electrified. The locomotives get their electricity from the overhead line.
19754.m: Almost all Swiss trains run on electricity.

19755.q: Who built the first usable battery around 1800?
19755.e: The Italian Alessandro Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with cardboard soaked in salt water. This “voltaic pile” supplied electricity continuously for the first time.
19755.m: The first battery was the voltaic pile.

19756.q: What voltage does a normal household socket in Switzerland supply?
19756.e: In Switzerland and throughout Europe the mains voltage is 230 volts alternating current. For large appliances such as cookers there are 400-volt connections.

19757.q: Who invented the lightning conductor in the 18th century?
19757.e: Around 1752 Benjamin Franklin showed that lightning is an electrical discharge. His lightning conductor carries lightning safely into the ground.
19757.m: A lightning conductor carries lightning into the ground.

19758.q: A device with a resistance of 46 ohms is connected to 230 volts. What is the current?
19758.e: According to Ohm's law, current equals voltage divided by resistance. 230 V divided by 46 ohms gives 5 A.
19758.m: Current is voltage divided by resistance.

19759.q: Which of these materials conducts electricity very well?
19759.e: Metals like copper have lots of free-moving electrons. That is why electric cables are usually made of copper inside.
19759.m: Copper is a very good electrical conductor.

19760.q: Which inventor championed alternating current in the so-called War of the Currents in the 1880s?
19760.e: Nikola Tesla developed alternating current systems together with George Westinghouse. Edison, on the other hand, backed direct current, but alternating current won out for power grids.
19760.m: Power grids today work with alternating current.

19762.q: How were sounds transmitted in the early telephone?
a: As electrical signals along a wire
19762.e: A microphone turned the sound waves into electrical signals. These travelled along a wire and became sounds again at the other end.
19762.m: The telephone transmits sounds as electrical signals.

19763.q: Who developed the alphabet of dots and dashes for the telegraph that is named after him?
19763.e: Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail developed a code of short and long signals. It meant messages could be sent over telegraph lines.
19763.m: Morse code is made up of short and long signs.

19764.q: What is the mobile phone traditionally called in Switzerland?
19764.e: “Natel” was originally short for “Nationales Autotelefon” (national car telephone). The name is still used for mobile phones in Switzerland today.
19764.m: In Switzerland people often call a mobile phone a Natel.

19765.q: In which year did Martin Cooper make the first public call with a handheld mobile phone?
19765.e: In 1973 Martin Cooper made a call in New York with a handheld mobile phone that weighed about one kilogram. It was many more years before there were small mobiles for everyone.
19765.m: The first mobile phone call took place in 1973.

19766.q: What does the abbreviation SMS stand for?
19766.e: SMS stands for “Short Message Service”. A single SMS can be no more than 160 characters long.
19766.m: An SMS is a short text message.

19767.q: Roughly how long did it take to make the oldest surviving photograph around 1826?
19767.e: The early processes were not very sensitive to light. That is why the plate had to be exposed for many hours before a picture appeared.
19767.m: The first photos needed hours of exposure.

19768.q: What were the first photographs captured on?
19768.e: In the daguerreotype, the picture was formed on a silver-plated copper plate. Paper prints and film came later.
19768.m: The first photos were made on metal plates.

19769.q: What is a dark room with a small hole, through which an image of the outside world falls on the wall, called?
19769.e: Camera obscura is Latin for “dark room”. It is the basic principle of every camera.
19769.m: Every camera is based on the camera obscura.

19770.q: How does the picture appear in a simple pinhole camera?
19770.e: The light rays cross in the small hole. That is why top ends up at the bottom and left ends up on the right.
19770.m: In a pinhole camera the picture is upside down.

19771.q: What replaces the old-fashioned film in a digital camera?
19771.e: The image sensor is made of millions of light-sensitive cells. It turns light into electrical signals, which are stored.
19771.m: In a digital camera the image sensor captures the light.

19772.q: What does the aperture of a camera control?
a: How much light comes through the lens
How big the image file is
19772.e: The aperture is an adjustable opening in the lens. A large opening lets in a lot of light, a small one only a little.
19772.m: The aperture decides the amount of light.

19773.q: How many pixels does a photo of 4,000 by 3,000 pixels have?
19773.e: You work out 4,000 times 3,000 and get 12,000,000 pixels. That is 12 megapixels.
19773.m: The number of pixels is width times height.

19774.q: Which brothers held one of the first public film screenings with paid admission in Paris in 1895?
19774.e: Auguste and Louis Lumière presented their Cinématographe on 28 December 1895. This day is often seen as the birthday of cinema.
19774.m: The Lumière brothers are seen as the fathers of cinema.

19775.q: Why do we see smooth movement when single pictures are shown quickly one after another?
a: The eye and brain join the pictures together
The pictures move on the screen
19775.e: Our visual system can't see very quickly changing pictures one by one. The brain joins them into a flowing movement.
19775.m: A film is made of lots of single pictures shown quickly.

19776.q: How many frames per second does a classic cinema film show?
19776.e: Since the days of sound films, cinema has used a standard of 24 frames per second. This looks smooth to the eye.
19776.m: A cinema film usually shows 24 frames per second.

19777.q: How many single frames does a 2-minute film at 24 frames per second have?
19777.e: 2 minutes are 120 seconds. 120 times 24 makes 2,880 frames.
19777.m: The number of frames is the length in seconds times the frame rate.

19778.q: What was new in cinemas from the end of the 1920s?
19778.e: Before that there were only silent films, often with a pianist playing along. From 1927 sound films with speech and singing took over.

19779.q: What is the animation technique called in which figures are moved slightly and photographed frame by frame?
19779.e: In stop motion a figure is moved a little after each photo. When played back, it looks as if it is moving by itself.
19779.m: Stop motion is made from lots of individually photographed scenes.

19780.q: In front of which wall are actors often filmed so the background can be changed on the computer later?
19780.e: The computer recognises the even green colour and replaces it with a different background. Green hardly appears in skin tones.
19780.m: With a green screen you can change the background.

19783.q: What is the force called that lifts an aeroplane upwards through its wings?
19783.e: The curved wings deflect the air downwards. This creates an upward force that carries the aeroplane.

19784.q: Which engine sucks in air, compresses it, burns kerosene and pushes hot gases out of the back?
19784.e: A jet engine creates thrust by pushing gases out of the back at high speed. Almost all large airliners use it.
19784.m: Large airliners fly with jet engines.

19785.q: Which Swiss solar aeroplane flew around the Earth without fuel from 2015 to 2016?
19785.e: Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg took turns flying Solar Impulse 2 around the world. The electricity came only from solar cells on the wings.
19785.m: Solar Impulse 2 flew around the world on solar energy alone.

19786.q: Who was the first to fly alone and non-stop across the Atlantic in 1927?
19786.e: Charles Lindbergh flew the “Spirit of St. Louis” from New York to Paris. The flight took about 33 hours.
19786.m: Charles Lindbergh crossed the Atlantic alone in 1927.

19787.q: What colour is the flight data recorder that is often called the “black box”?
19787.e: Flight recorders are usually bright orange so that they are easier to find after an accident. They record flight data and conversations in the cockpit.
19787.m: The black box is actually orange.

19788.q: What was the name of the first artificial satellite to orbit the Earth in 1957?
19788.e: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 into space on 4 October 1957. The metal ball sent radio signals back to Earth.

19789.q: Who was the first person to fly into space in 1961?
19789.e: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin orbited the Earth once in Vostok 1. The flight lasted about 108 minutes.
19789.m: Yuri Gagarin was the first person in space.

19790.q: Who was the first Swiss person to fly into space in 1992?
19790.e: Claude Nicollier from the canton of Vaud flew on the Space Shuttle Atlantis in 1992. Altogether he went into space four times.
19790.m: Claude Nicollier was the first Swiss astronaut in space.

19791.q: On which principle can a rocket fly even in the vacuum of space?
19791.e: The rocket pushes hot gases out of the back with great force. As a reaction it is pushed forwards, so it doesn't need air.
19791.m: A rocket flies on the recoil principle.

19792.q: Which Swiss university built the solar wind sail that was set up on the Moon during Apollo 11 in 1969?
19792.e: The University of Bern's solar wind sail caught particles from the solar wind. It was the only non-American experiment on the Apollo 11 mission.
19792.m: An experiment from Bern was already on the Moon in 1969.

19793.q: Who built the first working program-controlled computer, the Z3, in 1941?
19793.e: The German engineer Konrad Zuse built the Z3 from relays. It already calculated using the binary system.
19793.m: Konrad Zuse built the Z3 in 1941.

19794.q: Who is seen as the first computer programmer in history?
19794.e: Around 1843 Ada Lovelace wrote a program for Charles Babbage's planned calculating machine. The programming language Ada is named after her.
19794.m: Ada Lovelace wrote one of the first computer programs.

19795.q: Which two digits does the binary system of computers use?
19795.e: Computers work with two states, for example power on or off. These are shown as 0 and 1.
19795.m: Computers calculate with the digits 0 and 1.

19796.q: How many bits are there in a byte?
19796.e: A bit is the smallest unit of information. Eight bits together make a byte.
19796.m: A byte is made of eight bits.

19797.q: Which decimal number is the same as the binary number 1011?
19797.e: From the right, the places have the values 1, 2, 4 and 8. You work out 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 and get 11.
19797.m: In the binary system, the place value doubles to the left.

19798.q: Which programming language did Niklaus Wirth develop at ETH Zurich around 1970?
19798.e: Niklaus Wirth created Pascal mainly for teaching. He received the Turing Award in 1984 for his work.
19798.m: The programming language Pascal comes from Zurich.

19799.q: Which component, the “brain” of the computer, carries out the instructions of programs?
19799.e: The processor, also called the CPU, calculates and controls the processes in the computer. Modern processors manage billions of steps per second.
19799.m: The processor is the computer's calculating centre.

19800.q: Who invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989?
19800.e: The Briton Tim Berners-Lee wanted to make it easier for researchers to share documents. For this he developed linked web pages and the language HTML.
19800.m: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web.

19801.q: In which area is the CERN research centre, where the web was born?
19801.e: CERN is in Meyrin near Geneva, on the border with France. It is one of the largest research centres for particle physics.
19801.m: The World Wide Web was born in Switzerland.

19802.q: Since when have there been the first computer networks from which the internet grew?
19802.e: From 1969 the first university computers in the USA were connected to each other. This later developed into the internet.
19802.m: The forerunners of the internet appeared in the late 1960s.
